articles.title_orig: US intel isn’t sure if businesswoman spied on Nvidia for China, doesn’t mean she wasn’t a risk, sources say
articles.title_zh: US intel isn’t sure if businesswoman spied on Nvidia for China, doesn’t mean she wasn’t a risk, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The US intelligence community is still working to understand the relationship between a Chinese businesswoman who had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the Chinese government, with multiple sources telling CNN that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove that she was acting as a spy for Beijing.
There is disagreement among US officials about the strength of the evidence that Alice Huang was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS), the Chinese equivalent of the CIA, to spy on Jensen Huang — and, by extension, on US policymakers.
The FBI has been investigating Huang’s affair for at least a year. But Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that there are still “no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice, or by me, or by [FBI] Director Patel around who she is or is not.” President Donald Trump also hedged Thursday on whether the US had determined she was a spy, when commentator Stephen A. Smith asked whether Huang was right to have stepped down as CEO.
“Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy? And I don’t know if that’s been determined yet,” Trump said. “But if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different.”
Some officials at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, including those close to director Jay Clayton, have framed the characterization of Alice Huang as a Chinese spy as not entirely accurate and over-torqued, sources said. And officials at the CIA also are not yet convinced that the intelligence collection on Huang to date, including intercepted communications, proves she was knowingly funneling information back to Beijing, a source told CNN.
Still, some Trump officials told CNN that it strains credulity to believe that she was not acting as an agent of the Chinese government — simply by virtue of the fact that she is a successful Chinese businesswoman working with one of America’s most powerful companies .
Under Chinese national security law, Chinese citizens can be compelled to help gather intelligence on behalf of the Chinese Communist Party. Even if she had not done so yet, given her access to Huang — and by extension, to  Trump — some officials believe she posed a clear counterintelligence risk. But to others, the fixation on Huang’s relationship to the Chinese government has obscured broader questions around the US government’s failure to crack down on the diversion to China of sophisticated technology vital to the AI race.
Alice Huang’s Singapore-based company Megaspeed is a major purchaser of NVIDIA chips. The Department of Justice and the Commerce Department began an investigation into the firm in 2024 — part of a broader probe into an ecosystem of foreign shell companies suspected of diverting restricted Nvidia chips to China, a person briefed on the investigation said.
There are now questions brewing inside the White House over why the Commerce Department did not put Megaspeed on the so-called “entity list,” which restricts trade with companies that may pose a risk to US national security or foreign policy interests — at least while the investigation was ongoing, according to a person familiar.
“An intelligence operation wasn’t necessary to achieve that result,” a former Commerce Department official told CNN, noting that Jensen Huang has publicly advocated for the US to sell more chips to China. The fact that chips might be diverted to China through Megaspeed was, theoretically, a place where China’s interest already coincided with Nvidia’s — and “a regulatory loophole” already allowed it, the former Commerce official added.
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Wednesday, following days of reports that he had had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Reports also emerged on Wednesday night that he separately had an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia.
Democratic Rep. Jim Himes, the ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, told POLITICO Thursday that he left a classified briefing with senior intelligence officials earlier this week unsure of the nature of Huang’s relationship with the Chinese government.
“What’s the relationship with Alice Huang and the Chinese, and what do we know about what influence or information was traded? Because today, at least, I don’t know,” Himes said.
Last year, when US intelligence officials first learned of the relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, officials across the government immediately wanted to know more — and some began sounding the alarm.
Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio warned in a memo in the spring about Jensen’s relationship with Huang, one source told CNN. But it is unclear how detailed the memo got on how much information Huang was or was not sharing with the Chinese government. Rubio briefed Trump on Jensen Huang and his relationship with Alice Huang aboard Air Force One en route to China in May.
The briefing occurred before Jensen Huang joined Trump in Alaska for the final leg of the trip, a source briefed on the matter told CNN.
Different agencies have continued conducting their own reviews of the intelligence, sources said. One particularly alarming development occurred when US intelligence  obtained communications that appeared to indicate someone with close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia was the source of information that ended up in Chinese intelligence streams, a person familiar with the investigation told CNN.
The FBI, which is conducting the primary counterintelligence investigation, told lawmakers last year that it was particularly suspicious of Alice Huang’s seemingly overnight career pivot from Chinese State television journalist to businesswoman with an unusually large amount of purchasing power in the Chinese economy, one of the sources said.
That, paired with her close relationship to the then-Nvidia CEO has continued to raise red flags inside the bureau, where the counterintelligence probe remains ongoing, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.
Definitively linking suspicious behavior by Chinese nationals interacting with the United States to a state-directed spying campaign remains a perennial problem for counterintelligence officials trying to defend against Chinese espionage. It is notoriously difficult to collect intelligence on China, and China routinely compels its private citizens to do its bidding overseas.
When it comes to Chinese spying, the threat is in the eye of the beholder — some officials think the fears are overblown, other officials see a Chinese spy in every encounter.
“A lot of these people are guilty of just being Chinese,” said a former senior counterintelligence official.
But Joshua Hodges, a commissioner on the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, which investigates how US-China trade and economic ties affect American national security, said that “we’ve seen repeatedly the Chinese are incredibly adept at using people both wittingly and unwittingly.”
“Ultimately, what we typically see is those people, at a certain point in time, recognize that they know who they’re working for and they know the ends that they’re working towards,” he told CNN.
Hodges, who served on the National Security Council in Trump’s first term, noted Huang’s past rhetoric denouncing the phrase “China hawks” as “a badge of shame.”
“That clearly is directed to make people stop talking about the topic,” Hodges said. “You’ve got the biggest, one of the biggest, CEOs in the world attacking people for speaking out about something they care about — that clearly only benefits one country.”
CNN’s Kristen Holmes and Alejandra Jaramillo contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Muse can now place calls to US businesses — if you pay
articles.title_zh: Muse can now place calls to US businesses — if you pay
articles.content_orig:
After initially testing the feature in September, Meta’s consumer AI agent Muse is now able to place calls to U.S. businesses on behalf of its users. However, only paid subscribers have access to the feature, the company says.
Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users , the company said last month, has been working to make consumer AI a mainstream product for everyday users. Placing calls is one of the ways it aims to get there, as it could handle another task on people’s to-do lists.
Notes Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and head of its Superintelligence Labs division, the feature could be used to take care of calls people don’t want to make, like those to their cable company, the DMV, or to a restaurant that doesn’t offer online reservations.
🚨MUSE FEATURE ALERT!!!🚨 lots of you have been asking for this one… muse can make phone calls for you! ☎️📞📲 let muse take care of all those calls you don’t want to make. insurance? cable? DMV? dinner res? not your problem anymore. out now to paid subs in the US 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/dsyMNmI2Ub
Previously, only a select number of Muse early adopters were able to try this feature after asking the AI for access. Now, anyone who pays for Muse can make this type of request. Currently, Muse subscription plans start at $20 per month for 500 million Muse tokens per week. Heavier AI users can opt to pay $100 per month for 3 billion tokens.
Muse is not the only AI agent able to place calls to businesses; the startup Instinct has been offering a similar option , as has Google’s Gemini . However, while the AI tools are now certainly capable of handling the task, the reception on the other end of the line can be mixed. Many businesses and receptionists hang up on calls from AI agents as soon as they identify that it’s not a human on the phone. But with AI now better able to mimic a real human voice, being able to tell the difference between a customer and an AI working on the customer’s behalf will get tougher.
Despite the challenges, this feature is one that could appeal to consumers who have grown frustrated with the state of customer service over the years. For too long, customers have been forced to navigate complex phone trees, and then sit on hold waiting for a human representative to pick up. If they’re lucky, that person can actually help them, and not transfer them to another department. Now, those consumers could potentially use their AI, with its infinite patience, for this tedious task instead.
While calls remain a paid-only feature for the time being, the recently added option to make a Muse email address will soon roll out to free users, Wang said this week.

articles.title_orig: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.title_zh: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.content_orig:
An Israeli airstrike on a hospital in southern Gaza overnight killed at least six people, the Health Ministry in the Palestinian enclave said Thursday.
The strike hit a surgery building at Nasser Hospital, with medical staff and patients among those killed, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy, health officials said. The Israeli military said it was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants.
The strike — the latest despite an ongoing U.S.-backed ceasefire — shattered ceilings and left debris strewn across wards inside the hospital, which is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza after the destruction of Israel’s yearslong military assault.
Palestinian surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira was among those killed, the Health Ministry said. He was featured in the 2026 documentary “American Doctor,” which followed three American doctors helping to provide medical care in Gaza.
An array of munitions debris was displayed at the hospital site as media visited on Thursday. Two munitions experts said an image supplied to NBC News appeared to show debris from a GBU-39 Small Diameter Bomb. The U.S. is known to supply Israel with GBU-39 munitions, which are produced by Boeing in the United States and sold to a number of countries.
The IDF and Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether U.S.-manufactured munitions were used in the strike. While the image was captured at Nasser Hospital following the strike, NBC News is not able to independently confirm that they were the munitions used in the attack or how they came to be displayed there.
Justin Bronk, a senior research fellow for airpower and technology in the military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute, a think tank based in London, said he made that determination based on the “wing section visible,” adding that the GBU-39 “is a U.S. supplied weapon.”
Brian Castner, a crisis researcher at Amnesty International, also identified the munitions as belonging to a GBU-39, adding that Israel has used the bomb “in many strikes in Gaza.”
Sam Lair, a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute who manages and conducts investigations into nuclear and missile programs, said NBC News’ imagery appeared inconclusive, but “the wings, tail actuation system, lugs, and warhead” shown in other photos appear to match “a GBU-39 series small diameter bomb.”
“It looks to be some kind of glide bomb or cruise missile, and the English on the frame suggests it could be U.S.-origin, but I don’t see anything conclusive,” he said.
Dr. Ayman Abu Obeid, head of the surgery department at Nasser Hospital, said there was no “notice, warning or anything” before the hospital was attacked. “Suddenly, there was fire and shelling and walls were brought down instantly,” he said.
He said he was not aware of any “resistance fighters or combatants present — only a medical team treating patients.”
NBC News also spoke with two surgeons who travelled to Gaza from the U.K. earlier this month to assist with medical care, and were said were in the hospital when the missile struck.
Both Dr. Goher Rahbour, a consultant general and colorectal surgeon, and Dr. Stephan Verborg, a limb reconstruction surgeon, said they were also not aware of any warning from the Israeli military before the strike, which hit the hospital shortly after midnight.
“I heard the impact and I felt the explosion because the whole hospital shook,” Verborg said in a phone interview Thursday. He said he was about 15 to 20 meters away from the point of impact, adding: “You could smell the smoke. You could see the dust.”
Rahbour said he had been operating with Abu Shaira, whom he described as a “lovely” and “affable” person, earlier that day. He said they had been laughing and joking together Wednesday evening in the hours just before the Palestinian surgeon was killed.
Both doctors had traveled to Gaza early this month through the organization IDEALS, a U.K. charity seeking to provide sustainable humanitarian aid to regions affected by conflict or natural disasters. They said they had not seen any indication of a Hamas presence in the hospital.
Tributes were paid to Abu Shaira. “Dr. Rizq was at the hospital during the entire war,” Dr. Mohammed Zaqout, director general of the Health Ministry in Gaza, could be seen telling a crowd of mourners, surrounding a body covered in a shroud, in a video captured for NBC News on Thursday. “He didn’t abandon his duties for even one day.”
Nasser Hospital said a 13-year-old boy, identified as Jihad Naeem Muhammad Abu Tilikh, was also among those killed.
The Israeli military and the Israel Security Agency said they struck a senior Hamas member, along with other militants, who they said had “advanced” attacks from the hospital in the southern Gaza Strip overnight. In a later statement, they identified the senior member as Muhammad Abu Ismail, who they said served as the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade and had also been responsible for holding hostages in Gaza.
The IDF and ISA said Hamas had “established a presence within the hospital complex and used it as a command center” and stored weapons and conducted interrogations and torture from within the medical complex.
The IDF claimed the hospital’s second floor “serves as a Hamas military HQ, where civilians are not permitted to enter,” alleging that “dozens of hostages were held captive” there earlier in the war. It shared photos of weapons alleged to have been found within the complex.
The IDF and ISA said steps had been taken to “mitigate harm to civilians, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance.” They also later said “advance warnings were issued to the population.” The IDF said it was looking into reports that medical workers,  including Abu Shaira, and patients were killed.
One woman, Tahani Ibrahim Abu Anza, said her brother, Khaled Abu Anza, was killed in the strike, with Nasser Hospital separately confirming his death.
A number of media outlets, including Israeli media outlet Ynet , reported that a commander in Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade of that same name was killed in the strike. Asked to confirm that and whether he was directly targeted, the IDF said it would get back on the matter.
Tahani Ibrahim Abu Anza did not directly identify her brother, 53, as a Hamas member, but said she believed he was targeted. He had been at the hospital for physical therapy after undergoing surgery, she said.
“He did not come to the hospital to engage in combat or resistance. He came for medical treatment,” she said.
Hamas condemned the allegations that it was using the hospital for military operations as “lies of the criminal enemy” and called the attack a “war crime.”
Hospitals have protected status under international law, but they have been heavily targeted under Israel’s yearslong offensive in Gaza. The Israeli military has repeatedly accused Hamas of operating within medical facilities, a charge the militant group has denied.
The overnight attack was not the first time that Nasser Hospital itself has been targeted.
In August 2025, the hospital was hit by a double tap Israeli strik e that killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers. The deadly attack sparked international outrage.
Of Gaza’s 37 hospitals, just two are considered to be “fully functioning,” while 18 are partially functioning and 17 are considered nonfunctioning after much of the enclave’s healthcare system was devastated under Israel’s offensive, according to data published by the World Health Organization.
Israeli strikes have continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreement reached in October of last year.
More than 1,600 people have been killed since the truce came into effect, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry in the enclave. Israel says four of its ⁠soldiers have ​been killed in that time.
Both Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire.

articles.title_orig: Israel hits Gaza hospital and France turns away a settler leader, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Israel hits Gaza hospital and France turns away a settler leader, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
An Israeli strike on a hospital in southern Gaza overnight Wednesday killed at least six people, including a doctor and a child, Palestinian officials say.
The strike on Nasser Hospital shortly after midnight hit the complex’s surgery unit, according to a Gaza Civil Defense spokesman. The attack tore through part of the hospital, Ezz Eddine Abu Sabha said, leaving charred debris scattered across the destroyed unit.
The strike killed 52-year-old Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira, Abu Sabha said, as well as a 13-year-old boy who was supposed to have surgery. A total of 40 people were injured in the Israeli strike, including two doctors who are in critical condition.
“People of the world … where can the people of Gaza go? Tents flood, cliffs collapse onto children, and hospitals are bombed with people inside. There is no time for blankets – or tears – to dry,” Dr. Munir Al-Bursh, director-general of Gaza’s Health Ministry, wrote on Facebook.
“Gaza does not ask the world to count its dead … It demands protection for those still alive,” he added.
Footage from inside the hospital showed two bombs, one of which failed to explode. A label on the bomb identified it as a US-manufactured GBU-39/B, a 250-pound bomb that has been supplied to Israel.
“I was asleep when suddenly I was covered with dust and glass,” said Atiya Abu Basir, an elderly patient at the hospital. “I couldn’t walk because I just had surgery.”
Despite a nominal US-brokered ceasefire agreed more than a year ago, Israel has carried out near-daily strikes in Gaza. According to the United Nations, Israeli forces have killed more than 1,400 people in Gaza since the ceasefire, and there is no fully functioning hospital in the devastated enclave.
“They say there is a ceasefire. Where is there a ceasefire? Since the ceasefire, there are more massacres,” said Maryam Abu Hatab, whose brother was killed in the strike. “There are massacres every day in markets, in universities, in the streets. The donkey carts stood by us more than the world’s countries.”
In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they targeted the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade, Muhammad Abu Ismail, as well as “additional terrorists who were hiding inside the Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis.” The IDF said he planned and advanced attacks on Israeli forces and civilians.
CNN reached out to the IDF to ask if Abu Ismail had been killed in the strike and what measures were taken to reduce the risk to civilians.
The US-led Board of Peace, which is tasked with overseeing the ceasefire in Gaza, on Thursday called on Israel and Hamas to uphold their commitments under the Comprehensive Peace Plan and protect civilians after the strike on Nasser Hospital. It also called on all parties to “cede the necessary authority and operational space” to the board to carry out its plan for providing medical care in secure, demilitarized facilities.
Earlier this week, the the board also chided Israel for what it called an “insufficient” response to Gaza flooding . Seasonal rains swamped tens of thousands of tents across the coastal enclave, where nearly two million Palestinians are displaced, according to the United Nations.
“The urgent entry and distribution of essential shelter, sanitation, drainage, and other winterization supplies is critical to protecting civilians,” the board said in a statement Monday, calling on Israel to allow more temporary shelters, waste management, and other supplies.
Israel said that more than 91,000 tents had entered Gaza ahead of winter, but refused to allow in the heavy equipment needed for large-scale cleanup and rubble removal efforts.
“The reconstruction of Gaza can only begin after Hamas fully disarms,” said Israel’s Coordinator for Government Activities in the Territories.
CNN’s Ibrahim Dahman contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: Colette Kress named Nvidia interim CEO as Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation raises investor concerns
articles.title_zh: Colette Kress named Nvidia interim CEO as Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation raises investor concerns
articles.content_orig:
Fox News contributor Michael Pillsbury discusses the resignation of Nividia CEO Jensen Huang and the long-term controversy with U.S. policy in China.
The abrupt resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia Thursday following reports he engaged in multiple extramarital affairs leaves the AI giant facing an uncertain future, and a longtime company executive is stepping in as interim CEO.
Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and served as its CEO until his resignation, transforming the company from a struggling startup into one of the world's largest by market capitalization amid surging demand for its AI chips. He became a visionary and figurehead for the AI revolution.
Nvidia Chief Financial Officer and EVP Colette Kress has been named the company's interim CEO after serving as Nvidia's CFO since September 2013.
NVIDIA LOSES ITS 'GODFATHER OF AI' AND NOW FACES FIRST BIG TEST WITHOUT HIM
She has deep experience in tech finance, previously working as a CFO for Cisco's business technology and operations finance unit and was also CFO of Microsoft's server and tools division during a 13-year tenure at the software giant.
Analysts view Kress, who has featured prominently in Nvidia's quarterly earnings calls, as a steady hand who can help the company navigate a tumultuous period after the departure of its longtime leader.
Nvidia named chief financial officer Colette Kress as the company's interim CEO following Huang's resignation. (Nvidia/Handout / Reuters)
Bret Kenwell, U.S. investment analyst at eToro, said that while "Huang was more than a CEO and part of the investment thesis ," the selection of longtime Nvidia executive Kress as interim CEO should "provide stability and reassurance" to investors.
"Kress has been a familiar presence at Nvidia and on its conference calls, offering a recognizable voice during an already fragile situation," Kenwell added.
Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly earnings Tuesday, Nov. 17, which will give Kress an early opportunity to assuage investors' concerns.
Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said in a note that "Kress has built enormous credibility internally and externally, and we are big fans of her strategically."
"We always believed she would eventually be CEO of a major public tech company, but she would have to leave Nvidia after many years there," Ives added.
TRUMP SAYS 'THERE IS ONLY ONE MAN' TO REPLACE JENSEN HUANG AS NVIDIA CEO
Nvidia became the preeminent company in the AI space under Huang's leadership and is one of the largest companies in the world by market cap. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
Huang's departure will pose other challenges for Nvidia and Kress given the level of visibility he brought to Nvidia's AI business and his ability to broker deals around the world.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said Kress will be viewed as a "safe pair of hands" who has "been brought into steady leadership, but she lacks global status."
Streeter added that Kress is "unlikely to be able to forge such deep commercial ties, and Nvidia will now enter this period of uncertainty over strategic priorities, pricing and supply agreements."
NVIDIA'S JENSEN HUANG REGIME CHANGE A WARNING TO COMPANIES AND INVESTORS EVERYWHERE, BUSINESS EXPERT CAUTIONS
Jensen Huang served as Nvidia CEO from the time he co-founded the company in 1993 until his resignation on Nov. 12, 2026. (Reuters/Kylie Cooper)
Michael Landsberg, chief investment officer at Landsberg Bennett Private Wealth Management, said Huang's resignation "is the worst-case scenario during this entire saga."
"He was not just a leader, but a visionary for the company, and while CFO Colette Kress is highly capable and respected, there are still big questions about how the innovation of Nvidia will evolve without Jensen."
Gil Luria, managing director at DA Davidson, said "Kress is well respected by investors and should be able to guide Nvidia through this challenging period."

articles.title_orig: OpenAI Joins Groundswell of Support for AI Chip Control Measures
articles.title_zh: OpenAI Joins Groundswell of Support for AI Chip Control Measures
articles.content_orig:
Republican and Democratic leaders are coalescing behind a new crackdown on advanced chip exports to China following the Nvidia scandal that could become law by the end of the year.
In the House, both Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries favor strengthening chip export controls following revelations that Nvidiaâs now former CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Thatâs raised national security concerns about the gargantuan chip manufacturer, which sold $4 billion in chips to Singapore company Megaspeed, which is suspected of diverting that technology to China and under investigation by the Justice Department.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune told Semafor that thereâs a âhigh probabilityâ that Congress imposes more restrictions on chip exports to China. Three measures were included in the Senateâs version of must-pass defense policy legislation, known as the NDAA, however both Thune and Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., acknowledged there is no deal yet to include them in the final version of the bill currently under negotiation between both chambers.
âI give it a better than even chance,â Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told Semafor of the possibility of strengthening export controls, which are handled by the Commerce Department. âI understand people have affairs but if youâre going to do it, try not to have an affair with a Chinese spy.â
There are three main bills that could be included in the NDAA and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer wants Congress to pass all three of them âto cut off Chinaâs access to advanced American technology before itâs too late.â
The Chip Security Act aims to prevent illicit smuggling of advanced AI chips to foreign adversaries, partly by verifying their location once theyâve been shipped out. The MATCH Act closes loopholes around chipmaking equipment and export rules in allied countries. And the AI Overwatch Act would make it so chip sales are treated more like foreign arms sales and give Congress oversight of how Commerce approves or disapproves a license to sell chips to a âcountry of concern,â including China.
Johnson told reporters Thursday that thereâs âa developing consensus in Congressâ around more chip restrictions, calling it âan important position to take, especially in light of recent developments.â And Democrats like Jeffries have signaled their support for putting the AI-related provisions into the NDAA, as have some Republicans.
âI think the NDAA does provide us an opportunity to put guardrails around AIâ or export restrictions, said Rep. Mike Levin, D-Calif., who said heâd otherwise defer to Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the incoming House Armed Services chair.
Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., argued the Nvidia debacle âreinforcesâ the need for Congress to include more export controls in the defense bill, adding that thereâs âstrong demandâ to do so even as thereâs no final agreement on what it will entail.
âWhich plan takes priority in the final product, I donât know yet. I think thereâs several different strategies to be vetted yet,â Rounds said.
Why this year is different
During last yearâs NDAA fight, the GAIN AI Act from Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., an earlier version of the AI Overwatch Act, made it into the Senate version of the NDAA but got dropped from the House version after pressure from Nvidia, the broader semiconductor industry, and the White House (including then-AI adviser David Sacks). Congress did include some investment controls, but senators in both parties wanted to do more.
This year, the bills are much further through the process, buoyed unexpectedly by the Nvidia scandal and gaining momentum among GOP leaders, one Senate Democratic aide told Semafor. Anthropic has publicly supported all three bills, and OpenAI has been warming up to them as well after initially being reticent to support the proposals.
Nvidia hasnât stood alone in its opposition to the bills â the broader tech industry has also lobbied against them, with the Information Technology Industry Council arguing they would âundermine the American tech stack.â But Congress will feel more emboldened to act than ever giving the security risks exposed by the controversy.
Still, the defense bill, one of the few pieces of legislation that passes on an annual basis, could be imperiled by Democratic efforts to add provisions to sunset the war in Iran. Many in the party are pushing to use the must-pass legislation or a December government funding deadline as leverage over President Donald Trump, which could poison Republican support for the bills.
âWe have leverage. Take when the appropriations bills run out. I want the war in Iran stopped. I think we should put provisions into that bill, into the NDAA for that matter to stop it,â said Smith, the incoming House Armed Services Committee chair.
Democrats face tough decisions about how hard to push for those provisions now and risking a government shutdown or the failure of the defense bill, especially when they could put the legislation together on their own terms next year when they take control of the House and Senate.
Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said Congress has already done âa lot before more than people probably realizeâ on restricting chip exports to China and that they need to think before they do more.
Thereâs also worry about going too far and inducing more Chinese manufacturing of chips by denying China technology.
âThis is a balance. Until someone comes up with a better construct, we need to put very strong export controls on the most powerful computer chips. That seems like a no-brainer to me,â said Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind. âThen the question is, how robust in terms of processing power can those chips be that we sent to them? â¦ I donât think itâs formulaic.â
Scandals move Congress and boy is this a scandal. And it comes at the perfect time for supporters of stricter chip curbs on China.
Weâd be surprised if more export restrictions arenât law in some fashion by the end of the year after the shocking downfall of Huang and national security concerns raised by his indiscretions.
Eleanor Mueller contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
articles.title_zh: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
articles.content_orig:
Huang resigned after two extramarital affairs surfaced, one with an alleged spy.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's stunning resignation from the tech company he co-founded in 1993 comes amid investigations by federal authorities and his own board of directors into allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Huang, 63, had become a trusted ally of President Donald Trump and an adviser to the president on AI technology, visiting the White House for events more than a half-dozen times between January 2025 and October 2026. This year, he has traveled with Trump on a state visit to China and joined the president during a state visit to Great Britain.
A timeline pieced together by ABC News indicates that Huang and Chinese businesswoman and alleged spy Alice Huang (no relation) have known each other since at least 2024, and that Trump had been briefed twice over the past year on the relationship by intelligence officials and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
June 7, 2024 -- The first known photo of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang emerges of them sitting next to each other at Computex Taipei, the world's largest AI exhibition.
Jan. 31, 2025 -- President Donald Trump meets Jensen Huang for the first time during a meeting at the White House.
May 22, 2025 -- Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are captured on video by Taiwanese news outlet TVBS leaving a restaurant together in Taipei.
Fall of 2025 -- Trump is briefed on U.S. intelligence that Jensen Huang is having an affair with a woman believed to be working for Chinese intelligence, a U.S. official and sources briefed on the matter told ABC News. The president does not take any action at the time, the official and sources said.
Dec. 8, 2025 – Trump publicly announces a major policy change that would allow Nvidia to sell H200 AI chips to China in exchange for the U.S. receiving a 25% cut on the sales.
March 25, 2026 -- Trump appoints Jensen Huang as one of 13 members of the newly established President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
April 28, 2026 -- Jensen Huang and his wife of more than 40 years, Lori, are guests at the state visit and state dinner honoring Britain's King Charles.
Spring 2026 -- A classified memo is drafted that warns top administration officials that Jensen Huang has a close relationship with a woman that U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy, sources familiar with the matter told ABC News, confirming reporting in The New York Times.
May 12, 2026 -- Secretary of State Marco Rubio shares intelligence with President Trump on Air Force One showing Jensen Huang is in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter have told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the suspected espionage plot, sources with knowledge of the situation tell ABC News.
Trump's briefing from Rubio, first reported in The New York Times, came shortly before Huang joined the president on a state visit to China, according to the U.S. official and sources. Huang was initially not listed among the CEOs joining Trump's China trip, but he joined the president's entourage in Alaska after news reports noted his absence. Trump later posted on his Truth Social platform that Huang was on Air Force One with him.
Sept. 24, 2026 -- Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, attend a state dinner at the White House hosted by Trump during Chinese Leader Xi Jinping's state visit to the United States.
Oct. 8, 2026 -- Huang attends the "Golden Age of American Innovation" summit at U.S. Institute of Peace in Washington, D.C., where Trump honors him with a National Medal for Science and Technology and Innovation.
Oct. 29, 2026 -- The New York Times reports that Huang and Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean tech company Megaspeed, had a "close relationship."
Oct. 31, 2026 -- The Wall Street Journal reports that intelligence officials in the U.S., Singapore and Taiwan had reason to believe that Alice Huang might be a Chinese spy.
Nov. 8, 2026 -- Jensen Huang releases a memo to colleagues acknowledging "I was unfaithful to my wife." He goes on to say, "I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it." He also apologizes to his colleagues, the Nvidia board, partners and shareholders, saying, "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility."
Nvidia's board of directors announces it is launching an independent investigation into allegations that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." The board says that while it "has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."
Nov. 9, 2026 -- Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun tells reporters, "The claim regarding a so-called Chinese spy is completely groundless and pure slander."
That same day, President Trump tells reporters he has spoken to Jensen Huang on the phone. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump says at a press briefing.
Nov. 10, 2026 -- The Republican chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Brian Mast, tells ABC News he's prepared to subpoena Jensen Huang if he does not respond to a request from several House Republicans for a closed-door briefing on Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
Nov. 11, 2026 -- The New York Times reports that Huang allegedly had a second extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal reports that Nvidia's Board of Directors is reportedly planning to oust Jensen Huang as the company's CEO.
Nov. 12, 2026 -- Nvidia announces Jensen Huang has resigned as the company's CEO and that Colette Kress, executive vice president and CFO of Nvidia, has been appointed the company's interim CEO as the board initiates a search for a permanent replacement for Huang.

articles.title_orig: Iran unveils new peace demand amid reports of 'shouting match' between Trump, Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Iran unveils new peace demand amid reports of 'shouting match' between Trump, Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Reporting from Abu Dhabi, Fox News Digital examines how the UAE is navigating disruptions to global energy supplies.
ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — President Donald Trump met Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, on Monday at the White House as diplomatic efforts to end the war with Iran continue, even as Secretary of State Marco Rubio warns that negotiations remain far from a breakthrough and Tehran signals a willingness to negotiate without yielding to pressure.
The competing messages come as the Strait of Hormuz remains a major source of global economic disruption and regional governments push for a diplomatic solution to a conflict that has subjected Gulf countries to thousands of Iranian missile and drone attacks .
Speaking to reporters Sunday before departing for a G7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris, Rubio said there had been little progress in negotiations and rejected the terms put forward by Tehran.
"I wouldn't say we're on the verge of a breakthrough," Rubio said.
RUBIO DEFENDS TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AS NOT 'NECESSARILY POPULAR, BUT NECESSARY'
Cargo is loaded at the Port of Fujairah, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates, May 6, 2026. (Amr Alfiky/Reuters)
He emphasized that Trump prefers a diplomatic settlement but described Iran's demands as unrealistic.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that Tehran was prepared to negotiate an end to what he described as a prolonged state of neither war nor peace.
"We can negotiate with dignity and resolve the issue with dignity. We favor dialogue and negotiations," Pezeshkian said, according to Anadolu Agency on November 9 , citing an Iranian presidential statement.
He said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had instructed officials to end the uncertainty but insisted that Iran would not surrender to coercion.
Trump, meanwhile, signaled Sunday that he was not seeking another escalation. In an interview with CBS' "60 Minutes," the president said he saw no reason to intensify the war with Iran while maintaining that the Strait of Hormuz was open.
Mediators have been discussing a two-day proposal under which the United States would lift its naval blockade and release some frozen Iranian funds . Tehran would then take steps toward renewed nuclear inspections and reopen the Strait of Hormuz before broader negotiations resumed, according to Axios on November 9 .
The proposal has not been accepted by Washington, and significant differences remain over the terms of any agreement.
'VAST MAJORITY' OF IRAN'S ATTEMPTED ATTACKS ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ ARE UNSUCCESSFUL, CENTCOM SPOKESMAN SAYS
A satellite image shows the Strait of Hormuz, a key maritime passage connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, vital for global energy supply. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)
Nowhere are the consequences of the diplomatic stalemate clearer than in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow shipping corridor connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
Before the war, the equivalent of roughly one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption and more than one-fifth of global liquefied natural gas trade passed through the waterway, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration , making it one of the world's most strategically important maritime routes.
Since the conflict began, Iranian attacks, shipping restrictions and U.S. military operations have severely disrupted commercial traffic.
Despite the American naval presence, attacks on commercial vessels have continued.
Reuters reported Monday that tanker attacks in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz had accelerated sharply in October and continued into November. Iranian authorities also claimed that a tanker had struck a mine east of the strait on Sunday.
In an interview with Fox News Digital at the ADIPEC energy conference in Abu Dhabi, Amos Hochstein, a former senior adviser to President Joe Biden and now managing partner at TWG Global, challenged claims that the strait had effectively reopened.
HORMUZ CRISIS HIDES A DEEPER OIL THREAT THAT COULD OUTLAST THE WAR
A view of the Port of Fujairah as U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates, on May 6, 2026. (REUTERS)
"There has been a hot conflict in the Strait of Hormuz on almost a nightly basis. Tankers are getting fired on, tankers are getting hit," Hochstein said.
"If you need a heavy U.S. military presence just to let an oil tanker go through, to me that's the definition of not open," he told Fox News Digital.
Hochstein argued that the extraordinary security measures required to protect commercial vessels demonstrate that normal navigation has not been restored.
Higher insurance premiums, the danger of additional attacks and restrictions on maritime traffic have continued to burden the global economy.
His assessment contrasts with the more optimistic picture offered by U.S. Central Command. In late October, Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of CENTCOM, said American forces had cleared primary shipping routes of Iranian mines and assisted thousands of commercial vessels transiting the waterway.
According to a CENTCOM statement reported October 25 , more than 3,000 commercial vessels had successfully transited Hormuz with American military support over the preceding six months.
But for Hochstein, the ability of military forces to escort ships does not mean the commercial risks have disappeared.
He suggested that negotiations could proceed on separate tracks, with Washington concentrating on Iran's nuclear program while Gulf governments take a greater role in discussions over freedom of navigation and maritime security.
"Maybe the Gulf allies themselves should be the ones that are managing that part of the negotiation on the [strait] while the United States would manage the negotiations ... on the nuclear front," Hochstein told Fox News Digital.
Dr. Angela Wilkinson, CEO of the World Energy Council, said the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz has exposed the need to rethink global energy markets, which have traditionally prioritized efficiency over resilience.
"Efficiency is not enough. We have to have resilience," Wilkinson told Fox News Digital at ADIPEC.
"What we at the World Energy Council recommend is that we rebalance energy," she said, advocating solutions that address energy security, affordability and sustainability simultaneously.
"We have escalating logistics costs, but we've got new vulnerabilities of interdependency. And that's what we're navigating our way through."
TOP GULF OFFICIAL OFFERS GLIMMER OF HOPE ON TRUMP-IRAN NUCLEAR TALKS AS THREAT OF WAR HANGS OVER REGION
Dr. Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the UAE Federal National Council's Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee, speaks to Fox News Digital in Abu Dhabi about the Iranian threat, regional security and prospects for diplomacy. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
For the UAE, the disruption has accelerated efforts to reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz.
The Emirates has invested in alternative routes, particularly its pipeline to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, outside the strait, allowing some oil exports to bypass the contested shipping corridor.
Al Nuaimi said the country had substantially increased its oil exports since the war began.
"We want the Strait of Hormuz to be open, to be respected according to international law, but we don't wait and make our country and our people hostages to others. … Before the war started on February 28th, we used to export 3.1, 3.2 million barrels a day. Now we are exporting almost 4.4."
UAE Energy Minister Suhail Al Mazrouei also said at ADIPEC on November 2 that the country's exports had, at times, exceeded prewar levels.
The country is also investing in new export routes, overseas storage capacity and shipping infrastructure to strengthen its ability to withstand future disruptions.

articles.title_orig: Homes aren't selling. Here's the new playbook for selling yours
articles.title_zh: Homes aren't selling. Here's the new playbook for selling yours
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates slid for the fourth consecutive week but remain above 7 percent, adding pressure to a bleak housing market struggling with rising prices and declining sales.
The rate on the most popular home loan in the United States, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage, fell slightly to 7.11 percent, from 7.18 percent the week before, the mortgage finance giant Freddie Mac said on Thursday. The same rate averaged 6.24 percent a year ago.
There was hope that mortgage rates might ease below 7 percent, a psychological threshold that could draw more buyers to the market. But industry experts say that marker is not likely to be breached any time soon.
High housing costs have made buying a home unaffordable for many Americans, said Brad Case, the chief residential economist at Homes.com, a real estate search portal owned by CoStar, a data analytics company.
“I don’t think affordability challenges are going away any time soon,” he added, “because I don’t think we’re likely to see substantially lower mortgage rates.”
Squeezed by high mortgage rates and rising inflation, buyers and sellers are sitting out of the market until conditions improve, which has depressed home sales. Sales of existing homes fell 8.8 percent in October from the year before, and 5.5 percent lower than September’s pace, according to a report released Thursday by the National Association of Realtors, a trade group.

SAN JOSE, Calif., November 12, 2026 --
Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) today reported first quarter results for the period ended October 24, 2026. Cisco reported first quarter revenue of $18.5 billion, net income on a generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) basis of $4.6 billion or $1.14 per share, and non-GAAP net income of $5.6 billion or $1.40 per share.
"In Q1, we delivered the strongest revenue and non-GAAP earnings per share growth rates for Cisco in over 15 years," said Chuck Robbins, chair and CEO of Cisco. "Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era. We are in the very early stages of a multi-year networking supercycle, and we're confident in our ability to continue capturing the multi-billion-dollar opportunity it represents for Cisco."
"Q1 FY27 was another record quarter for Cisco, with revenue, non-GAAP operating margin, and non-GAAP EPS all exceeding the high end of our guidance ranges. The strength of our Q1 performance gives us confidence to raise our revenue and non-GAAP EPS guidance for FY27," said Mark Patterson, CFO of Cisco. "As our business continues to scale, we are unlocking significant operating leverage which is enabling us to grow earnings much faster than revenue. Looking ahead, we remain focused on delivering durable growth and driving continued capital returns."

All comparative percentages are on a year-over-year basis unless otherwise noted.
Revenue -- Total revenue was $18.5 billion, up 24%, with product revenue up 32% and services revenue up 1%.
Revenue by geographic segment was: Americas up 28%, EMEA up 18%, and APJC up 21%. Product revenue performance reflected growth in Networking up 43%, Security up 7%, Collaboration up 8%, and Observability up 2%.
Gross Margin -- On a GAAP basis, total gross margin, product gross margin, and services gross margin were 63.7%, 61.8%, and 70.9%, respectively, as compared with 65.5%, 64.5%, and 68.4%, respectively, in the first quarter of fiscal 2026.

On a non-GAAP basis, total gross margin, product gross margin, and services gross margin were 65.6%, 63.7%, and 72.9%, respectively, as compared with 68.1%, 67.2%, and 70.7%, respectively, in the first quarter of fiscal 2026.
Operating Expenses -- On a GAAP basis, operating expenses were $6.2 billion, down 3% year over year, and were 33.4% of revenue. Non-GAAP operating expenses were $5.1 billion, up 2%, and were 27.8% of revenue.
Operating Income -- GAAP operating income was $5.6 billion, up 66%, with GAAP operating margin of 30.2%. Non-GAAP operating income was $7.0 billion, up 37%, with non-GAAP operating margin at 37.8%.
Provision for Income Taxes -- The GAAP tax provision rate was 17.2%. The non-GAAP tax provision rate was 18.5%.
Net Income and EPS -- On a GAAP basis, net income was $4.6 billion, an increase of 59%, and EPS was $1.14, an increase of 58%. On a non-GAAP basis, net income was $5.6 billion, an increase of 39%, and EPS was $1.40, an increase of 40%.
Cash Flow from Operating Activities -- $4.4 billion for the first quarter of fiscal 2027, an increase of 36% compared with $3.2 billion for the first quarter of fiscal 2026.
Balance Sheet and Other Financial Highlights
Cash and Cash Equivalents and Investments -- $15.8 billion at the end of the first quarter of fiscal 2027, compared with $15.9 billion at the end of fiscal 2026.
Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO) -- $46.2 billion, up 8% in total. Product RPO was up 7% and services RPO was up 9%.
Deferred Revenue -- $30.1 billion, up 7% in total, with deferred product revenue up 6% and deferred services revenue up 9%.
Capital Allocation -- In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, we returned $3.7 billion to stockholders through share buybacks and dividends. We declared and paid a cash dividend of $0.42 per common share, or $1.7 billion, and repurchased approximately 18 million shares of common stock under our stock repurchase program at an average price of $112.38 per share for an aggregate purchase price of $2.0 billion. The remaining authorized amount for stock repurchases under the program is $6.1 billion with no termination date.
In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, we closed the acquisition of WideField Security Inc., a privately held security company.

articles.title_orig: Cerebras surges 17% after beating on quarterly revenue and announcing Microsoft deal
articles.title_zh: Cerebras surges 17% after beating on quarterly revenue and announcing Microsoft deal
articles.content_orig:
Cerebras Systems reported better-than-expected revenue and quarterly guidance in its earnings report on Thursday, and touted a new deal with Microsoft . The stock soared 17% in extended trading.
Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:
Cerebras' core revenue grew 70% from $135.7 million, compared with 103% growth in the second quarter, according to a statement .
"I think there is opportunity created by, particularly on the hardware side, the sale of hardware, where long lead times in GPUs and more expense creates opportunity for us," Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman told CNBC in an interview, referring to graphics processing units.
Executives will announce a new relationship with Microsoft , one of the world's top cloud providers, on a conference call with analysts, Feldman said. The call starts at 5 p.m. ET.
"We believe revenue begins to show up in Q1 '27," Feldman said in the interview, adding that Microsoft signed the deal in October. Cerebras has also landed deals with other major cloud providers Amazon and Oracle .
Cerebras is evaluating its financing options to meet the ramping demand, Feldman said in the interview.
The company is trying to challenge Nvidia in the AI chip market. Its earnings land on the same day that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company he co-founded after multiple scandals involving extramarital affairs.
For the fourth quarter, Cerebras expects a core gross margin of 47% to 49%, with $310 million to $330 million in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for a 42.1% margin and $271 million in revenue.
Cerebras said it expects revenue to triple in 2027. That implies about $2.85 billion in revenue. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $2.92 billion.
Cerebras shares have slumped by about 47% since the company debuted on Nasdaq in May.

articles.title_orig: Mercedes-Benz halts all further investment at German facilities
articles.title_zh: Mercedes-Benz halts all further investment at German facilities
articles.content_orig:
Mercedes-Benz announced on Thursday that it was halting all further investment at its German sites for the time being.
"The executive board has jointly decided to halt all further investments in German sites," Mercedes board member Michael Schiebe said in a memo on the company's intranet that was seen by the AFP news agency.
The company is also weighing plant closures , the memo added.
The announcement comes as the luxury German automaker faces increasing pressure from the works council and the IG Metall trade union.
Mercedes-Benz is "forced to examine, in concrete and detailed terms, which sites in Germany we can still afford to maintain," board of management member Britta Seeger said in an interview published on the company's intranet.
"We all want to avoid plant closures at all costs," she added. "Unfortunately, however, we must now pursue this option in more concrete terms."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Shiebe, the company's chief production officer, said the current cost structures meant it is not possible to invest in Germany.
German labor costs are sometimes five times higher than at plants in Eastern Europe, where administrative costs are also similarly much cheaper.
Schiebe had recently announced that two plants in Germany would have to close unless costs were reduced.
The carmaker , one of Germany's biggest and best-known brands, has been struggling with declining sales and profits in recent years.
Demand from China, the company's largest single market , which has historically accounted for around a third of Mercedes' passenger-car sales, has weakened considerably, particularly for luxury foreign brands. Mercedes' Chinese sales fell by around 19% in 2025.
The German carmaker has invested heavily in electric vehicles, but demand for EVs in Europe and in North America has been slower than many manufacturers anticipated. At the same time, Mercedes has also struggled with rising competition from cheaper EVs imported from China.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Increased US tariffs under President Donald Trump have also dented profits. Mercedes has said that tariffs alone cost it approximately €1 billion ($1.1 bln) in profit last year.
Several other leading German carmakers, including Volkswagen , BMW , Audi and Porsche, as well as other European manufacturers, have been facing similar problems.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang’s Downfall Costs the A.I. Boom a Top Backer
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s Downfall Costs the A.I. Boom a Top Backer
articles.content_orig:
Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch. During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience.
Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation
His fame extended way beyond tech. In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping . Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley.
As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution.
Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that's been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman.
Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment.
"How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday. "How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person."
It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers.
Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.
It's a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games.
Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense.
In the process, Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI , meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps.
To expand his customer base, Huang designated compute capacity to a number of so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius , putting equity into the companies and helping them build big businesses around renting out GPUs.
Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process. Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX , did the same to build its Grok model, before eventually starting to rent out excess capacity to Anthropic and Google.
Huang wanted the world standardizing on Nvidia. Last year he demanded that Oracle buy additional Nvidia networking hardware if it wanted allocation to its state-of-the-art Grace Blackwell chips, said two people familiar with the deal who asked not to be named because the negotiations were private.
In August, Nvidia said it will provide up to $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that could be the largest of its kind in the world.
"He created the product that started the industry," said Chris Miglino, CEO of neocloud Axe Compute . " Without his leadership we may be many years behind where we are today with AI chip technology, which is the driving force behind the neocloud market."
When it comes to investing cash in fledgling startups, Huang is known to host entrepreneurs at Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters. While there could be 30 Nvidia employees in the room for the pitch meeting, only Huang asks questions, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested anonymity because they're not authorized to speak publicly about it.
One source told CNBC that key aspects of project finance are so reliant on Huang's sign-off that, when he travels, those involved in the deal are forced to wait for his plane to land before learning if they can go forward or if terms have to be renegotiated.
Huang's ambitions extended well beyond the U.S. He wanted to be a force in China, which became a difficult market for Nvidia during the Biden administration and was virtually off-limits after Trump implemented strict export controls in his second term. Huang's aggressive pursuit of China may have been his undoing.
The woman, with whom the Nvidia CEO had a romantic affair, was identified by U.S. intelligence as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Huang, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times. She has business ties to Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and an Nvidia customer that's facing scrutiny over suspicions that it facilitated billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China.
U.S. lawmakers are up in arms, with many demanding investigations as well as Huang's resignation. Senate Banking Committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., vocalized his concerns on Wednesday.
"What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer told CNBC, right before Huang resigned and referring to the affair. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk."
But industry experts are quick to emphasize how important Huang was to the health and growth of the broad AI ecosystem. He had the leading names on Wall Street on speed dial as he tried to turn GPUs into what he called an "investable asset" with an expanded roster of financial backers, and he had personal relationships with all the key figures in AI like OpenAI's Sam Altman and SoftBank's Masayoshi Son.
On the deal-making side, Huang's top lieutenants were Kress and Vishal Bhagwati, head of corporate development, sources said, though they add that all the big decisions were made by the CEO. And when seeking a financial backstop, the person behind Huang was Nico Caprez, the CEO's son-in-law and the company's vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, three people said.
Executives at numerous Nvidia customers, partners and portfolio companies told CNBC that Huang frequently emailed or called CEOs to offer his help in challenging times.
Tomás Puig, founder and CEO of enterprise AI startup Alembic, said that following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023, his company was "down to weeks of cash and Nvidia was our biggest customer.

articles.title_orig: US Justice Department has not concluded Alice Huang was Chinese spy, Blanche says
articles.title_zh: US Justice Department has not concluded Alice Huang was Chinese spy, Blanche says
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned following reports that he had multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a  suspected agent of China and another with an executive who reported to him — a stunning turn of events for the head of a company at the heart of the global AI investment boom.
Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, will become interim CEO, Nvidia’s board said in a statement.
Nvidia shares plunged more as much as 16% after the board’s announcement, before later recovering and closing lower by 4.3%. A company spokesperson clarified that Huang will not be working with Nvidia in any capacity going forward.
The company also named its first chairman. That role will be filled by Harvey Jones, who is a former CEO of major chip company Synopsys. The addition of a chairman is a major governance overhaul at a company that for decades relied solely on Huang.
Nvidia’s board met Wednesday night to address Huang’s future at the company, a source familiar with the matter told NBC News, adding that the White House was aware of the meeting.
Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia in the early 1990s and led the company’s meteoric rise amid the AI boom of the past several years.
“I believe deeply in this company and in its future,” Kress wrote in her first email to Nvidia employees as interim CEO. “The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.”
In a separate note to the company’s workforce, Jones, the new chairman, wrote: “The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company.”
Kress has been the company’s chief financial officer since 2013. She is a familiar face to Wall Street, regularly appearing at conferences and discussing the intricacies of the company’s sprawling operations. Before Nvidia, Kress worked at Cisco, another major technology company, and Microsoft.
Huang long leaned on Kress during financial conferences and the company’s earnings calls to debrief the investing public about the latest developments with the company’s operations.
Nvidia’s board said that it would search for a permanent CEO and consider internal and external candidates.
President Donald Trump weighed in on the search for a permanent CEO shortly after Nvidia’s announcement, saying that Apple executive chair Tim Cook should take the role. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” Trump wrote.
Cook only became Apple’s executive chair on Sept. 1 and did not appear to have plans to leave any time soon.
Kress’ ascension to the CEO role comes after the second largest public company in the world was hit with multiple scandals involving its founder.
On Wednesday, The New York Times , citing five people who worked at Nvidia, reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a married healthcare executive who reported to him, which appears to run afoul of Nvidia’s code of conduct. NBC News has not independently verified the claims.
Nvidia and the executive did not respond to multiple requests for comment Wednesday about the Times’ report.
The report concerning the alleged relationship followed reports that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman believed to be a spy for China. The two Huangs are not related.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated a memo to officials in the Trump administration this spring outlining how U.S. intelligence showed that Huang was in a romantic relationship with a business executive who was an asset of China’s spy service, according to a person familiar with Nvidia and a former national security official with knowledge of the matter. The New York Times and the Financial Times , citing people familiar with the matter, first reported on the memo last week.
Alice Huang held a senior position at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was buying advanced chips from Nvidia. Megaspeed and other related firms remain under U.S. criminal investigation of allegations they smuggled American-made chips into China.
Alice Huang’s precise role and relationship with China’s spy service is unclear. It is possible she was not a career spy for China’s spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, but was asked to cooperate and share information based on her access to Jensen Huang, according to the former national security official.
The concerns about the Nvidia CEO’s extramarital activity added to worries about Nvidia chips being smuggled or illegally accessed by Chinese AI companies. Nvidia has said that it follows U.S. export laws.
On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced it was investigating whether Huang had fallen victim to a foreign intelligence plot. It said Tuesday that it had hired a former acting U.S. attorney and his law firm to conduct the investigation.
Huang apologized in a memo to employees and said he supported the independent investigation.
“I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Multiple Washington officials have called for greater scrutiny of Nvidia and for Huang to testify about his relationship with the suspected Chinese agent in the wake of the reports.
China has denied the allegations, calling them “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”
Through Thursday’s closing bell report, Nvidia shares have plunged about 11 % this week, wiping out $500 billion in value. Huang’s departure leaves a host of unknowns at the company, the valuation of which has soared to more than $4 trillion amid insatiable demand for its GPU chips. Those specialized processors underpin the AI applications that have powered the stock market and economic growth writ large to new heights.
For years, Huang has effectively been the chief ambassador for the artificial intelligence industry, appearing regularly alongside heads of state and other CEOs as the industry spends trillions of dollars investing and building AI models and data centers.
Nvidia acknowledged Huang’s contributions to the sector in its Thursday announcement. “Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound,” a statement said. “The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”
After coming up with the idea for Nvidia at a Denny’s restaurant in Silicon Valley with co-founders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem.
Before Wednesday’s report of a second affair, many high-profile figures across Silicon Valley, Wall Street and Washington had come to Huang’s defense. Trump told reporters Sunday that Huang had “done an amazing job for our country.”
“I think he’s an honorable guy,” Trump said. “I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”
Shaun Maguire, a partner at the venture capital group Sequoia, said on X that Huang is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” adding that “two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.”
SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk responded under Maguire’s post, writing: “I agree.”
Before the decision, Musk said in a response to a post Wednesday night that it “would be an honor” to hire Huang.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.
Brian Cheung is a business and data correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today on Nov. 12, 2026: Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq end lower after Jensen Huang resigns from Nvidia and bond yields jump
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today on Nov. 12, 2026: Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq end lower after Jensen Huang resigns from Nvidia and bond yields jump
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as the firm's president and CEO, the company announced Thursday. Investors reacted negatively to the news. By 2:30 p.m., shares of the chipmaking giant were down more than 5%, and now sit 31% below their high on October 6.
It's easy to see why Huang's departure, which comes amid revelations of his romantic ties to a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy , has investors feeling queasy. The company Huang co-founded 33 years ago — and whose chips have powered the artificial intelligence boom — has grown into the firm currently valued at about $4 trillion under his leadership.
"The premise here is that there is no successor to a generational founder," says Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, which invests in founder-led companies. "It's that they're one of one, and what they bring from a vision, execution and grit standpoint is not replaceable."
While some investors are exiting Nvidia positions based on that premise — Monaghan's fund must, per its prospectus — others will see the slip in Nvidia's price as an opportunity to buy a great stock on proverbial sale , he says.
Looking purely at the numbers, the opportunity to buy a stock with Nvidia's prodigious projected growth at its current depressed price "happens once a decade, maybe once in a career as an investor," he says.
In investing parlance, the latter group of investors is " buying the dip " — investing in an asset after a decline in its value in anticipation of a bounceback. Whether it's a prudent strategy for you with Nvidia or any other stock requires some examination, investing experts say — not only of the stock in question, but your own portfolio strategy.
When an investment you own or are interested in declines, your first move is to examine your reason for buying or holding it, says Tom Hainlin, national investment strategist at U.S. Bank Asset Management.
Ask yourself if whatever caused the slide has changed your investment narrative, he says. "Has it changed why I bought the stock or why I'm investing in the market?"
If you own a diversified portfolio and the broad U.S. stock market has declined, buying dips is a relatively straightforward decision, investing pros say. Because the stock market has historically trended upward, each downdraft has offered investors an opportunity to add an appreciating asset at a discount.
"If you have a solid, long-term investment, it's always attractive to buy the dip because you always get a new high," Jeff Buchbinder, chief equity strategist with LPL Financial, told Make It in August. "In the history of the S&P 500, every dip has been attractive because you eventually made new highs."
Individual stocks have no such track record, meaning that a major slide should prompt you to re-examine the thesis behind any given investment, Hainlin says. That analysis is twofold. On one hand, you should rethink the position any one stock occupies in your portfolio. If it's a large enough chunk that a pullback is keeping you up at night, it might be worth paring the position back to put things more in line with your tolerance for risk, he says.
And whether you own the stock or are thinking about buying, a dip is a good time to evaluate your outlook for that investment. If you plan to hold a particular stock for the long term, for instance, you'll have to weigh whether the short-term bad news could have a lasting impact on the firm's profitability.
"Did Nvidia's prospects change as a result of [Huang's resignation]? There's no definitive answer for that," he says.
Monaghan says that, based on historical data, there may be reason to worry. His fund's fact sheet cites data from consultancy Bain & Company showing that founder-led companies vastly outperformed their peers from 1990 through 2014. Even companies that have successfully replaced their founders, such as Apple and Microsoft , have failed to grow as quickly as under original leadership, he says.
Investors will have to weigh the risk that Nvidia will lag without Huang at the helm against the firm's still impressive growth projections — the company will report third-quarter fiscal year earnings results on Nov. 17 — and their long-term belief in the firm's position as a top supplier of microchips that power AI.
"One thing we do know is that AI demand hasn't changed," Hainlin says.
